extracted.intended_audience: design-patent practitioners, litigators, and prosecutors (U.S. practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for prosecuting and litigating U.S. design patents after the Federal Circuit's Egyptian Goddess decision, covering infringement standards, claim construction, prior art use, jury instructions, and prosecution tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary observer test as the sole test for design-patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: “the ‘ordinary observer’ test should be the sole test for determining whether a design patent has been infringed.” (Egyptian Goddess, 543 F.3d at 678).  Gorham formulation: if, in the eye of an ordinary observer, giving such attention as a purchaser usually gives, two designs are substantially the same ... the first one patented is infringed by the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the overall-appearance comparison from the perspective of an ordinary observer (the attention a purchaser usually gives). This is the controlling doctrine for infringement; courts should assess whether two designs would appear “substantially the same” to such an observer rather than isolating discrete novel points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apply the 'point of novelty' test
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ‘point of novelty’ test should no longer be used in the analysis of a claim of design patent infringement.” (Egyptian Goddess).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should not base infringement proof on identifying and proving discrete points of novelty. Prior strategies that required patentees to specify points of novelty are displaced; instead focus on the ordinary-observer overall-appearance inquiry (though prior art remains relevant as described elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction: courts need not provide a detailed verbal description
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts have a duty to conduct claim construction in design cases but “need not attempt to provide a detailed verbal description of the claimed design, as is typically done in the case of utility patents.” (Egyptian Goddess, 543 F.3d at 679).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have discretion on the level of verbal detail. The preferable course is ordinarily not to construe a design patent by providing a detailed verbal description because verbalization risks placing undue emphasis on particular features and having the factfinder focus on individual described features rather than the design as a whole. Practitioners should be prepared to address potential prejudice if courts do verbal constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court guidance items that may bear on claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A trial court may guide the jury on a number of other issues that bear on the scope of the claim, including: describing the role of design patent drafting conventions, such as broken lines; assessing and describing the effect of representations made during prosecution; and “distinguishing between those features of the claimed design that are ornamental and those that are purely functional.” (Egyptian Goddess).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing scope or instructing juries, courts may explain drafting conventions (e.g., broken lines indicate unclaimed environment), discuss prosecution history statements, and identify functional vs ornamental elements. Practitioners should address these topics in motions and jury-instruction drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior art in the ordinary-observer analysis (‘in light of the prior art’)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary observer test has always been conducted “in light of the prior art,” “with reference to prior art,” or “in the context of the prior art.” (Egyptian Goddess, multiple citations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art can inform the ordinary-observer comparison; courts vary in how they apply this. If the patented design and accused product are plainly dissimilar, prior art may not be needed. Otherwise, compare claimed and accused designs to the prior art to inform whether an ordinary observer would find them substantially the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-level (threshold) analysis for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Many district courts have utilized a two level analysis: a level-one or ‘threshold’ analysis to determine if comparison to the prior art is even necessary, and a second-level analysis that accounts for prior art in less obvious cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level 1: ask whether the accused and claimed designs appear substantially similar (threshold). Level 2: if not plainly dissimilar, compare the claimed and accused designs alongside the prior art to determine whether an ordinary observer would still find them substantially the same. Courts disagree on specific tests (e.g., sliding-scale vs. observer-aware-of-prior-art approaches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden allocation: accused infringer bears production of prior art; patentee bears burden of proving infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The accused infringer bears the burden of prior art production because it is motivated to point out close prior art; the patentee still bears the burden of proof of infringement. (Egyptian Goddess: burden of production on accused; burden of proof remains on patentee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accused parties should search for and produce close prior art during discovery. Patentees must still prove infringement (preponderance of evidence) in light of any produced prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using prior art as a defense (practicing-the-prior-art defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practicing the prior art may be a defense to design patent infringement: an accused infringer may attempt to prove that their accused design is practicing the prior art. (Discussed as a post-Egyptian Goddess strategy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accused infringers can rely on prior-art production to show non-infringement or obtain summary judgment by demonstrating the accused design practices prior art. This is a tactical alternative to invalidity challenges, though factual nature of ordinary-observer comparison can make summary judgment harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using prior art to prove infringement (patentee strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee may use its own prior art to show the overall assimilability between the patented design and the accused design if the prior art is different than both the patented design and the accused design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees can present prior designs that place the patented design and the accused design in context (e.g., showing both are closer to each other than to other prior art) to help the ordinary-observer comparison. Example from text: lion (patent) vs tiger (accused) with elephant and giraffe as prior art may illustrate assimilability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare jury instructions early and consider IPO model instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed IPO Model Design Patent Jury Instructions define infringement as “an analysis as the ordinary observer in light of the prior art” and recommend early preparation of jury instructions in cases post-Egyptian Goddess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt or adapt model instructions early in discovery/strategic planning. The IPO draft includes three practical guidelines for juries: 1) when the claimed design is visually close to the prior art, small differences may be important; 2) if the accused design includes a claimed feature that departs conspicuously from the prior art, that may be important; 3) if the accused design is visually closer to the claimed design than to the closest prior art, that comparison may be important. (Appendix and Jury Instruction No. 8.3.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture claims (detailed figures) as a prosecution strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit design patent applications with “picture claims”—increased detail in figures to describe an article in detail—when competitors may copy the patented design in great detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picture claims can capture detailed features but risk creating design-around options and complicating infringement proofs (especially for articles with utilitarian function). Consider filing multiple applications with varying detail to avoid easy design-arounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portion practice: use of broken (dashed) lines and omission to limit claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Use broken lines to show environment or portions not intended to form part of the claimed design; draw distinctive portions in solid lines. Alternatively, omit less-important portions or views from figures to focus the claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broken lines effectively exclude elements from the claimed design (MPEP §1503.02; Egyptian Goddess noted role of broken lines). Omission of rear/bottom views can limit claimed scope to illustrated portions. These techniques change claim scope and can affect ordinary-observer analysis—examples include guitar-body/neck/headstock scenarios where broken vs solid lines alter infringement strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: File multiple applications to claim different elements/levels of scope
rubrics_metrics.description: File multiple design patent applications with varying degrees of coverage (detailed figures, broken lines, omitted features) to build a portfolio protecting one design concept at differing scopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple applications increase cost but can strengthen protection and flexibility in enforcement by providing patents with varying claim breadths to counter design-arounds and capture different infringing variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality and prosecution-history considerations may limit claim scope (district-court variance)
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts differ on incorporating functionality and prosecution history into claim construction: some courts (e.g., Richardson v. Stanley Works) remove functional elements in claim construction, while others (e.g., Depaoli v. Daisy Mfg.) defer functionality/prosecution-history limitations until later (summary judgment or jury instructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect differing district-court approaches: in some jurisdictions the court may identify and exclude purely functional elements at claim-construction stage; in others the court will avoid detailed verbal constructions to prevent undue emphasis and address functionality later. Anticipate and plan briefing to address which approach the court should take and how to demonstrate prejudice if detailed verbal constructions are used.
